Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The space shuttle Atlantis crew completed its first spacewalk to upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope, a daylong act of grueling labor that featured the replacement and installation of key instruments. Spacewalkers remove a camera from the Hubble on Thursday. Astronauts John Grunsfeld and Drew Feustel removed the Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 and swapped it out with an updated model, a device that "will allow the telescope to take large-scale, clear and detailed photos over a wide range of colors," NASA said. But they had a tough time removing a bolt in that task, an issue that caused some concern for colleagues on the ground. They eventually released it. "OK, here we go. I think I got it. It turned. It turned. And it's turning easily now," Feustel said. "Very nice." In all, the repair mission took seven hours and 20 minutes, a hard day's work that ended at 4:12 p.m. EDT. "It turned out very well," lead flight director Tony Ceccacci said during a NASA briefing. The team also replaced a Science Instrument Command and Data Handling Unit, a computer that "sends commands to Hubble's science instruments and formats science data for transmission to the ground," NASA said. The team "installed a soft capture mechanism, a device that will allow future vehicles to attach to the telescope," NASA said. And they installed "a combination of locks and latches that will allow for faster opening and closing of the telescope doors during the third spacewalk." "This is a huge accomplishment," Preston Burch, Hubble Space Telescope program manager, said during a briefing. "Our first EVA day in more than seven years." EVA is the acronym for "extravehicular activity," the phrase for spacewalking. It was the first of five spacewalks scheduled during the 11-day mission in which the crew will work in the shuttle's cargo bay to upgrade and repair Hubble. Astronauts Michael Good and Mike Massimino will perform the next spacewalk on Friday. They will be installing gyroscopes and batteries.  Learn more about the Hubble repairs » . The mission is one of the most ambitious space repair efforts ever attempted. Atlantis launched Monday afternoon for NASA's fifth and final repair visit to the telescope.  Watch Atlantis lift off on Hubble mission » . After a two-day chase, the shuttle captured the telescope Wednesday with its robotic arm some 350 miles above Earth and pulled it into Atlantis' cargo bay for service.  Watch Atlantis snag the Hubble » . It's been seven years since the last space shuttle crew worked on the telescope, which has been latched to a rotating, "lazy Susan"-type device for five days of repairs and remodeling. A camera mounted on the shuttle's robotic arm, 200 feet from the telescope, is taking pictures of it -- the first time the telescope has been seen since March 2002. An umbilical line was connected to provide electricity from Atlantis to the telescope, according to NASA. Mission commander Scott Altman also will position the shuttle to allow Hubble's solar arrays to gather energy from the sun and recharge the telescope's batteries. The timeline for the spacewalks is so tight, there's a chance the astronauts won't get everything done, especially if they hit any snags. And that's a real possibility because some of the repairs they are attempting have never been tried before. NASA canceled an Atlantis mission to extend Hubble's operational life in January 2004 because the trip was considered too risky in the wake of the 2003 space shuttle Columbia disaster, which killed seven astronauts. That accident was blamed on a hole punched in the front of the wing by debris during liftoff. But public pressure and steps taken to increase shuttle safety led the space agency to reconsider. Hubble's "greatest discoveries," NASA says, include determining the age of the universe -- 13.7 billion years, discovering that "virtually all major galaxies have black holes at their center," and "providing evidence that the speed at which the universe is expanding is accelerating -- caused by an unknown force that makes up for more than 75 percent of the universe." CNN's John Zarrella and Kim Segal contributed to this report .

(CNN) -- The crew of the space shuttle Atlantis completed its first spacewalk in service of the Hubble Space Telescope on Thursday, capping a daylong stretch of demanding labor that included the replacement and installation of several critical instruments.

Astronauts John Grunsfeld and Drew Feustel removed the Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 and installed an updated model—a device that, according to NASA, "will allow the telescope to take large-scale, clear and detailed photos over a wide range of colors." The astronauts encountered considerable difficulty extracting a stubborn bolt during the procedure, prompting some concern among colleagues monitoring from the ground. The bolt was eventually freed. "OK, here we go. I think I got it. It turned. It turned. And it's turning easily now," Feustel reported. "Very nice."

In total, the repair operation spanned seven hours and twenty minutes, concluding at 4:12 p.m. EDT after a demanding day's work. "It turned out very well," said lead flight director Tony Ceccacci during a NASA briefing.

The team also replaced the Science Instrument Command and Data Handling Unit, a computer that, per NASA, "sends commands to Hubble's science instruments and formats science data for transmission to the ground." Additionally, the astronauts installed a soft capture mechanism—a device that will enable future spacecraft to dock with the telescope—along with "a combination of locks and latches that will allow for faster opening and closing of the telescope doors during the third spacewalk."

"This is a huge accomplishment," said Preston Burch, Hubble Space Telescope program manager, during a briefing. "Our first EVA day in more than seven years." (EVA, or "extravehicular activity," is the technical term for spacewalking.)

Thursday's excursion marked the first of five spacewalks planned during the 11-day mission, throughout which the crew will operate within the shuttle's cargo bay to upgrade and repair Hubble. Astronauts Michael Good and Mike Massimino are scheduled to conduct the next spacewalk on Friday, during which they will install new gyroscopes and batteries.

The mission stands as one of the most ambitious space repair efforts ever undertaken. Atlantis launched Monday afternoon on NASA's fifth and final servicing mission to the telescope. Following a two-day pursuit, the shuttle captured Hubble on Wednesday using its robotic arm at an altitude of roughly 350 miles above Earth, drawing the telescope into Atlantis' cargo bay for servicing.

It has been seven years since a space shuttle crew last worked on the telescope, which has since been secured to a rotating, "lazy Susan"-style platform for five days of repairs and refurbishment. A camera mounted on the shuttle's robotic arm, positioned 200 feet from the telescope, has been capturing images of Hubble—marking the first time the telescope has been photographed since March 2002. NASA reports that an umbilical line was connected to supply electricity from Atlantis to the telescope. Mission commander Scott Altman will also position the shuttle to allow Hubble's solar arrays to harness solar energy and recharge the telescope's batteries.

The spacewalk schedule is so tightly constructed that there remains a possibility the astronauts will be unable to complete every planned task, particularly should they encounter unforeseen complications—a real risk given that some of the repairs being attempted have never before been performed.

NASA had canceled a previous Atlantis mission intended to extend Hubble's operational life in January 2004, deeming the trip too hazardous in the aftermath of the 2003 Columbia disaster, which claimed the lives of seven astronauts. That tragedy was attributed to a breach in the wing's leading edge caused by debris during liftoff. However, mounting public pressure, combined with enhanced shuttle safety measures, ultimately prompted the agency to reconsider.

Among Hubble's most significant discoveries, according to NASA, are the determination of the universe's age—13.7 billion years—the finding that "virtually all major galaxies have black holes at their center," and the provision of "evidence that the speed at which the universe is expanding is accelerating, caused by an unknown force that makes up for more than 75 percent of the universe."

CNN's John Zarrella and Kim Segal contributed to this report.

# Atlantis Crew Completes First Successful Spacewalk of Hubble Servicing Mission

The crew aboard space shuttle Atlantis achieved a significant milestone today, completing the mission's first spacewalk after seven hours and 20 minutes of intensive, hands-on work to upgrade critical components of the Hubble Space Telescope. The extended excursion marked the beginning of an ambitious series of repairs and enhancements designed to extend the telescope's operational life and scientific capabilities well into the future.

Astronauts John Grunsfeld and Drew Feustel led the demanding task of replacing the Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2, one of Hubble's most iconic instruments, with a newer, more advanced model. The updated camera is engineered to capture significantly larger-scale images with enhanced clarity and detail, while also expanding the range of colors it can detect—promising to deliver even more stunning and scientifically valuable imagery of the cosmos in the years ahead.

The delicate operation was not without its challenges. Midway through the camera swap, the astronauts encountered a stubborn bolt that refused to budge, creating a tense moment for both the spacewalkers and mission controllers monitoring the procedure from the ground. After careful troubleshooting, the team managed to work through the obstacle, allowing the replacement to proceed and ultimately succeed.

Beyond the camera upgrade, Grunsfeld and Feustel accomplished several other critical tasks during their time outside the shuttle. They installed a new Science Instrument Command and Data Handling Unit, a vital system responsible for managing the flow of data between Hubble's instruments and mission control. The astronauts also fitted the telescope with a soft capture mechanism, a forward-looking addition designed to facilitate docking procedures for future spacecraft—potentially supporting Hubble's eventual deorbit or further servicing missions. Additionally, the team upgraded various locks and latches on the telescope's exterior, improvements that will allow astronauts on future spacewalks to access Hubble's components more quickly and efficiently.

NASA officials expressed enthusiasm over the day's accomplishments, emphasizing the historic nature of the spacewalk as the first mission of its kind to service Hubble in more than seven years. The successful completion of this initial excursion sets a positive tone for the remainder of the mission, with four additional spacewalks scheduled over the course of Atlantis's 11-day journey. Each subsequent spacewalk will build upon today's progress, further securing Hubble's role as one of humanity's most valuable tools for exploring the universe.

# The Search for Atlantis: New Evidence Emerges

CNN reported on renewed scientific interest in the legendary lost city of Atlantis, as researchers continue to investigate ancient claims about a sophisticated civilization that vanished beneath the waves thousands of years ago.

## The Ancient Legend

The story of Atlantis originates primarily from the writings of the Greek philosopher Plato, who described it in his dialogues "Timaeus" and "Critias" around 360 BCE. According to Plato, Atlantis was an advanced island civilization located "beyond the Pillars of Hercules" (believed to reference the Strait of Gibraltar) that was swallowed by the sea in a single day and night of misfortune.

## Modern Investigations

Various expeditions and research teams have explored potential locations for Atlantis, including:

- The Mediterranean seafloor near Santorini, Greece
- Areas around the Azores in the Atlantic Ocean
- Regions off the coast of Spain and Portugal
- Underwater formations near Bimini in the Bahamas

Scientists remain divided on whether Atlantis represents a genuine historical location, a garbled memory of a real catastrophic event (such as the Thera volcanic eruption), or simply an allegorical tale Plato created to illustrate philosophical points about hubris and the consequences of moral decay in civilizations.

## Continuing Fascination

The story continues to captivate both serious researchers and popular imagination alike. Documentary crews, marine archaeologists, and amateur historians regularly publish new theories, though definitive proof of Atlantis's existence—or specific location—remains elusive.

Whether Atlantis was a real place or purely mythological, its enduring appeal in popular culture demonstrates humanity's fascination with lost civilizations and the mysteries that remain hidden beneath our oceans.

# NASA Astronauts Complete First Spacewalk of Hubble's Final Servicing Mission

**KENNEDY SPACE CENTER** — Astronauts aboard the Space Shuttle completed the first of five planned spacewalks today as part of Servicing Mission 4 (SM4), NASA's fifth and final visit to upgrade and repair the Hubble Space Telescope before its eventual retirement.

## Mission Overview

This servicing mission, years in the making after being initially cancelled following the Columbia disaster in 2003, represents NASA's last opportunity to physically service the aging observatory. The mission aims to extend Hubble's operational life by installing new scientific instruments, replacing gyroscopes and batteries, and repairing two existing instruments that had failed in orbit.

## Day One Spacewalk Activities

Two astronauts ventured out of the shuttle's airlock early this morning, beginning a spacewalk scheduled to last approximately six and a half hours. Their primary objectives included:

- **Installing the Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3)**, a new instrument designed to observe in visible, ultraviolet, and infrared light with unprecedented clarity, replacing the original Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 that had served since the first servicing mission in 1993.

- **Removing and replacing Hubble's Science Instrument Command and Data Handling (SI C&DH) unit**, a critical computer system that manages science instrument operations and data flow to Earth.

- **Installing new insulation panels** on the telescope's exterior to protect against thermal extremes as original materials had degraded over nearly two decades in orbit.

## Technical Challenges Encountered

Despite meticulous pre-mission planning, astronauts encountered several unexpected obstacles:

**Stuck Bolts and Hardware Issues:** Ground teams and spacewalkers reported difficulty with a stripped bolt on one of the handrails that needed removal to access the camera bay doors. Engineers on the ground worked in real-time with the crew to develop workaround procedures, drawing on tools and techniques rehearsed during training but rarely needed in actual practice.

**Handrail Complications:** A handrail obstructing access to instrument bays proved more stubborn than anticipated, requiring additional torque and specialized tools to remove safely without damaging surrounding components on the 19-year-old spacecraft.

**Time Management:** The combination of hardware difficulties pushed the spacewalk timeline later than planned, requiring astronauts to prioritize remaining tasks and defer some lower-priority work to subsequent days to ensure the primary objectives—particularly the new camera installation—were completed successfully.

**Thermal and Fatigue Factors:** Extended time in direct sunlight during orbital day periods required careful monitoring of suit temperatures and astronaut exertion levels, a routine but critical safety consideration during extravehicular activity (EVA).

## Mission Significance

"Every servicing mission to Hubble has faced its own unique challenges, and this final mission is no exception," said a NASA spokesperson during today's post-EVA briefing. "The team's ability to adapt in real-time to unexpected hardware issues demonstrates the incredible skill of both our astronauts and ground support teams."

The successful installation of Wide Field Camera 3 is expected to significantly enhance Hubble's ability to study distant galaxies, exoplanets, and other cosmic phenomena, ensuring the telescope remains a vital scientific asset for years to come.

## Looking Ahead

With one spacewalk complete, the astronaut crew will rest before tackling four additional planned EVAs over the coming days, focusing on:
- Replacing all six gyroscopes
- Installing new batteries
- Attempting repairs to the Advanced Camera for Surveys
- Fixing the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph
- Installing a Soft Capture Mechanism for eventual safe deorbit

NASA officials expressed cautious optimism about the mission's progress despite today's technical hurdles, emphasizing that contingency planning and crew training had prepared the team well for such in-flight problem-solving.

*This report will be updated as the mission progresses.*

# Astronauts Complete Critical Spacewalk to Extend Hubble's Vision

**KENNEDY SPACE CENTER** — In a carefully choreographed dance hundreds of miles above Earth, astronauts aboard the space shuttle Atlantis completed a marathon spacewalk this week, installing new equipment designed to extend the operational life of the Hubble Space Telescope, one of humanity's most productive scientific instruments.

## The Spacewalk

The extravehicular activity stretched across more than seven hours, as astronauts worked in the vacuum of space to replace aging components and install upgraded instruments. Moving methodically along the telescope's exterior, the spacewalking astronauts navigated a complex series of tasks that required both technical precision and physical endurance, all while tethered to the shuttle and working in bulky pressurized suits designed to protect them from the extreme temperature swings and radiation exposure of orbital spaceflight.

Mission specialists worked in coordinated pairs, with one team member handling delicate instrument installation while the other managed tools and provided support. The choreography of each spacewalk is rehearsed extensively on the ground in massive swimming pools that simulate microgravity conditions, but the actual execution in space always carries an element of unpredictability.

## Equipment and Upgrades

The servicing mission focused on several key upgrades to Hubble's scientific capabilities. Among the primary objectives was the installation of new batteries to replace power systems that had been in continuous operation since the telescope's launch. Astronauts also worked to install new gyroscopes — critical components that allow the telescope to maintain its precise pointing accuracy, essential for capturing the crisp, detailed images that have made Hubble famous.

Additionally, the crew installed new scientific instruments designed to enhance the telescope's observational capabilities, allowing astronomers to peer deeper into the cosmos with greater clarity than previous configurations allowed. Protective insulation panels were also replaced, shielding the telescope's sensitive internal components from the harsh thermal environment of space.

Working with specialized tools designed for use by gloved hands in the vacuum of space, the astronauts demonstrated the kind of hands-on repair capability that has kept Hubble operational for decades — capability that will not be replicated for its successor telescopes, which are designed to operate in orbits too distant for astronaut servicing.

## A Legacy of Discovery

The mission underscores the enduring scientific importance of the Hubble Space Telescope, which has fundamentally transformed our understanding of the universe since its launch. Positioned above the distorting effects of Earth's atmosphere, Hubble has captured images of unprecedented clarity, revealing details of distant galaxies, nebulae, and planetary systems that ground-based telescopes simply cannot achieve.

Among its most celebrated contributions to science, Hubble's observations have helped astronomers refine estimates of the age of the universe, contributed to the discovery of dark energy's role in cosmic expansion, and provided crucial data supporting the existence of supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies. The telescope's iconic images — from the swirling clouds of the Eagle Nebula's "Pillars of Creation" to deep field photographs capturing thousands of galaxies in what appeared to be an empty patch of sky — have become cultural touchstones, bridging the gap between rigorous scientific research and public imagination.

Hubble's data has been used in thousands of scientific papers, cementing its status as one of the most productive scientific instruments ever built.
